diagnostic_evidence.quote: E-AO and SRPL are instead designed to be fast heuristics, but they only converge to stationary points.

issues.failure_explanation: Stationarity does not imply local optimality here. Take A=diag(-2,-1,3) and P=Q=cone{e1,e2}. Starting both methods at the second generator leaves them at u=v=e2, with value -1. This is a stationary saddle: along u=v=(sin(t),cos(t),0), the objective is -1-sin²(t), whereas varying just one vector increases it. This example also survives preprocessing, since the global value is -2 rather than -||A||=-3.

failure_location.quote: The other two are heuristics, meaning that they rapidly compute locally optimal solutions; one uses an alternating projection algorithm with extrapolation, and the other a sequential partial linearization approach based on fractional programming.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace the local-optimality promise by an approximate-stationarity promise. Retaining local optimality requires an additional procedure or argument that rules out saddle termination.
issues.overall_effect: The advertised local-optimality guarantee for both heuristics is false, even on nontrivial instances remaining after preprocessing.
issues.title: The heuristics can terminate at saddles rather than local minima
issues.why_classification: The source-supported resolution changes the promised guarantee from local optimality to stationarity; neither supplied heuristic excludes saddles.

issues.failure_explanation: Pointedness is not assumed globally. For P=R×R_+, the unit vectors e1,-e1,e2 form a minimal conic generating set, but e2 lies in no one-dimensional face. The only one-dimensional face is the line R e1. Thus the two purportedly equivalent descriptions are incompatible on allowed cones.

failure_location.quote: A \textit{ray} of $P$ is any nonzero vector of a $1$-dimensional face of $P$,  or equivalently any positive multiple of the columns of $G$.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Distinguish minimal conic generators from rays, and restrict the asserted equivalence to pointed cones without restricting the algorithms themselves to pointed cones.
issues.overall_effect: The identification of all generator columns with rays is invalid in the stated general polyhedral setting.
issues.title: Minimal generators need not be rays of a nonpointed cone
issues.why_classification: A local correction of the geometric terminology preserves the generator-based constructions and their scope.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: Let  $(u,v)$ be a local minimum of $\MA(P, Q)$ with $u \neq -v$ in dimension $n\le 3$. Then $u$ or $v$ is a generator of its respective cone.

issues.failure_explanation: The cited corollary explicitly excludes antipodal pairs. In R³, let P have cross-section at z=1 equal to the square with vertices (±1,±1), and let -Q have the diamond with vertices (±3/2,0),(0,±3/2). Their intersection contains the z-axis, so the optimal angle is π. No generator of either cone belongs to the other cross-section, so no optimal pair contains a generator and the proposed searches miss the optimum.

failure_location.quote: As a consequence, the minimum over the optimal values of $\MA(\f R_+g_i,Q)$ and $\MA(P,\f R_+ h_j)$ over all $i,j$ correspond to the maximum angle of $\MA(P, Q)$.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: First apply the paper's antipodal-intersection preprocessing. Use generator enumeration only when the optimal value is not -1, and qualify the accompanying claim accordingly.
issues.overall_effect: Generator enumeration alone is not a complete solver in dimension three.
issues.title: The low-dimensional generator search omits antipodal solutions
issues.why_classification: An existing polynomial-time preprocessing step supplies a short bypass and preserves the advertised low-dimensional scope.

issues.failure_explanation: The feasible set is homogeneous and excludes only the zero image. Scaling any feasible z by t tending to zero makes the residual tend to zero, whether or not a nonzero zero-residual image exists. Thus the infimum is always zero and a minimum may not exist. For A=diag(2,1), P=R_+e2, and Q=-R_+e2, this infimum is zero although the original optimum is -1, not -||A||=-2.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Formulate the test as existence of a nonzero cone image with residual exactly zero, rather than as the value of the unnormalized minimization problem. The ensuing normalized ±1 feasibility tests can then be retained.
issues.overall_effect: The stated optimal-value characterization cannot distinguish the extremal case from nonattainment.
issues.title: The homogeneous optimal-value test always has infimum zero
issues.why_classification: The source already supplies normalized tests that implement the corrected attainability formulation.

issues.failure_explanation: The preceding convergence justification concerns ordinary alternating optimization. E-AO instead optimizes against extrapolated partners, so its accepted pair need not be a blockwise minimizer. Rejecting objective increases establishes only monotonicity of objective values. The source supplies no argument forcing steps to vanish or limit points to be critical, and beta can remain at one rather than tending to zero.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Use the already described ordinary AO, with beta fixed at zero, for the convergence-guaranteed variant. Keep E-AO as an empirically motivated heuristic unless a convergence proof or suitable additional safeguard is supplied.

issues.failure_explanation: At n=1 the Schur cone is {0}, so it contains no unit vector and the minimization has no feasible pair. The stated optimal value is therefore not attained, and the asserted unique pair divides by n-1=0.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: $\mc H:= \cone\left( \left\{e_i-e_{i+1} \right\}_{i=1,\dots,n-1}  \right) \cu \f R^n$

issues.failure_explanation: For n=2, the Schur cone is the single ray generated by e1-e2. Its only unit vector must be used for both x and y, so the minimum inner product is 1. The displayed formula instead gives cos(pi/2)=0.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Restrict the displayed formula to n≥3 and give the n=2 value separately as 1, corresponding to angle zero.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: {the matrix $N\in \mca N_n$ that maximizes the angle between $\mca N_n$ and $P$} is the negative part of $P$, that is, $N = P^-$.

issues.failure_explanation: Nonzero input does not ensure a nonzero negative part. For N=I, the first construction returns P=0; for P=I, the reverse construction returns N=0. Zero has no angle and cannot satisfy the unit-norm constraint. Thus these are not universal maximal-angle best responses as claimed.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Use normalized negative parts only when they are nonzero. Otherwise use a minimum-eigenvalue rank-one projector for the PSD response, or a minimizing normalized generator of the symmetric nonnegative cone for the nonnegative response.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: Second column: Largest known angle between $\mca P_n$ and $\mca N_n$.
Notice that we know the ground truth only up to dimension $23$. For higher dimensions, we report the best known values, obtained by letting Gurobi run for at least $24$ hours on each problem.
E-AO and SRPL are the only methods to converge to the optimum value within the $10$ seconds for all dimensions.
Sometimes, the algorithms may find larger angles than the best known angles, but it has to be attributed to rounding errors.

issues.failure_explanation: Matching the best known feasible angle does not certify optimality of the unrestricted matrix-cone problem. The same confusion appears for circulant dimensions 25 and 27, where the source explicitly has only best-known lower bounds but nevertheless calls the matching heuristic values optimal. Likewise, exceeding a best-known angle need not be rounding error; it may improve the bound.

failure_location.quote: In other words, $\MA(\mca P_n,\mca N_n)$ is often solved by a pair of block-circulant matrices, that is,  matrices with diagonal blocks, where all blocks are circulant.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Describe these results as matching or improving best-known feasible bounds. Reserve statements of optimality and inevitable rounding error for cases with an independent exact value or a certified matching upper bound.
